prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks based on magic-wavelength trapping of neutral atoms, reaching fractional uncertainties near 10^-18

statement.case_for: I have moved my preferred configuration from B053 to B057. In round 1 I ranked the clocks fourth and put topological insulators first on the grounds that a new organising principle outweighs a measurement advance. After the exchange I think that framing was less decisive than I made it, for two reasons. First, the credit problem for B053 is not a matter of wording. Kane and Mele gave the Z2 theory, Molenkamp's group observed the quantum spin Hall state, but Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang made the HgTe prediction that Molenkamp tested, and Hasan's ARPES work established the three-dimensional materials. With a hard ceiling of three people, any B053 prize leaves out someone whose omission the community would find hard to accept, and the 2016 prize on topological phases adds a conceptual overlap I cannot argue away. Second, my reservation about B057 was novelty against the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize. Kroll, Mehlig and Pearce have answered that convincingly: the comb is a tool for counting optical cycles and the 2012 prize concerned control of single quantum systems, whereas magic-wavelength trapping of many neutral atoms is a different physical idea whose point is to remove Doppler, recoil and light-shift errors while keeping the statistical power of thousands of atoms. The outcome, independently reproduced uncertainties near 1e-18, is new, and it feeds tests of constants and relativity and relativistic geodesy. Katori for the concept and first realisation and Ye for taking the strontium clock to record accuracy and stability is a pair that I can defend against every objection raised, which I cannot say for any three-name version of B053. As someone who computes electronic structure for a living, I also note that the clock result is reproduced across many laboratories with a well-understood systematic budget, which is the standard I apply to maturity.
statement.case_against: The reservation I carry into the vote is that a precision-metrology prize in this neighbourhood is the third in twenty years, so the citation must be tied tightly to magic-wavelength lattice trapping of neutral atoms and not to optical clocks or frequency standards in general; Ido and Kimble's earlier trapping ideas and the work of Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Bloom and the ion-clock groups are real contributions outside a two-name credit, and a prize is not a complete history. Topological insulators remain, in my view, the larger change to how a whole field organises its thinking, and routine computation of topological invariants in DFT workflows is part of my own daily practice, so I regret that the three-name limit prevents a clean credit. If the committee preferred a discovery that reorders a field to a refinement of a measurement, B053 would still be my choice, but I do not think the attribution can be made defensible.

responses.point: Kroll argued that the comb is a tool for counting optical cycles and not the discovery, that magic-wavelength trapping lets many neutral atoms be interrogated in parallel without Doppler, recoil or light-shift penalties, and that a prize is not a complete history so Katori and Ye are the defensible core.
responses.response: This answers my round-1 objection and it is the main reason I moved. I had treated the lattice clock as the culmination of a line already recognised in 2005 and 2012. Your distinction between a counting tool, control of single ions, and a many-atom architecture that gains stability from parallel interrogation is a distinction of physics and not only of framing. I also accept your point that unrepresented groups apply to nearly every candidate and should not block a two-name prize. Where I stay cautious is the citation: the committee should not use language that could be read to claim the comb or ion-clock work, and I agree with you that the lattice and the 1e-18 realisation should be named together.

responses.point: Mehlig argued that the overlap argument cuts in favour of the clock, because the comb made clocks readable and the ion prize made single-quantum control routine, but neither delivered the many-atom lattice architecture, and asked that the citation be framed around the lattice and magic wavelength.
responses.response: I find that persuasive and I adopt that framing for my own citation. It also fits what you said about the redefinition of the second, with which I agree with Kroll: the demonstrated agreement of independent clocks at the 1e-18 level is the achievement, and the redefinition is a later metrological decision that should not condition the prize. On your own first choice, I remain unconvinced that B025 can be separated from the 2021 prize without a clearer argument that its physical content, not its algorithmic reach, is the point, but I appreciate that you put the clock first after testing it for flaws and not because of the count.

responses.point: Lindroth challenged my B026 ranking, saying TMR is more of a continuation of the 2007 giant magnetoresistance prize than the lattice clock is of the 2005 comb prize, and that Parkin's role is optimisation and not discovery.
responses.response: Both points are fair and I no longer rank B026 first. The 1995 observations of Miyazaki and Moodera are decisive, but the 2007 prize already covers the spin-dependent transport and read-head story, and what made the devices commercial was MgO-barrier work that is more engineering, which is why Parkin sits uneasily in a trio. I keep B026 only as an alternative, and only if a citation could be confined to the 1995 discoveries, which then shrinks the credit. On B053 I share your concern about Bernevig, Zhang and Hughes, and my own attribution doubts there are now one reason I accept B057 rather than defending my round-1 choice.

responses.point: Danielsson replied to my ranking by asking which of the shortlisted candidates I think beats the clocks on clarity of discovery and attribution, and said B053 attribution is harder than the clock case.
responses.response: On the shortlist as it stands, none beats the clocks on clarity of attribution, and I concede that directly. B053 beats them on conceptual reach, but your question concerns attribution as well, and there I cannot make the case. I also agree with you that breadth of opening support should not decide the matter, and I do not move because seven colleagues did. I move because the attribution and overlap arguments hold up when I test them. I would add that your remark that the discovery side, not the metrology alone, is what makes this a physics prize is correct, since the comparison of independent clocks tests relativity and constants at a level not otherwise accessible.

responses.point: Pearce, as chair, moved from IceCube to B057 and argued that the 2005 prize rewarded the comb as a measurement tool and the 2012 prize control of single quantum systems, so the citation should name the lattice mechanism explicitly.
responses.response: I agree with the citation point and have written mine accordingly. I also share your concern, which you and others raised against B054 and that I raised in round 1, about isolating three names from a large collaboration with AMANDA, Baikal and DUMAND precursors. In answer to the chair's questions: I do not propose a third name for B057, I treat the redefinition of the second as irrelevant to timing, and a Hasan versus Mele choice no longer affects my preferred configuration because B053 is now an alternative. If B057 were set aside, I would support B053 only if the committee can accept the omission of Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, which I currently find difficult.

uncertainties: Whether a citation can be drawn tightly enough around magic-wavelength lattice trapping of neutral atoms that it neither claims the 2005 comb prize nor the 2012 single-quantum-system and ion-clock work.
Whether Ido and Kimble's earlier proposals for trapping at a magic wavelength and the contributions of Lemonde, Takamoto and others require wording in the citation even if they are not credited.

Whether the committee is too influenced by the disciplinary lens of its atomic physicists and by the apparent consensus, and whether a field-reorganising result such as B053 should be given more weight than I now give it.
Whether B053 could be repaired by a different three-name selection or by a two-name credit, which I cannot settle from the evidence supplied.
statement.conflict_note: I have no documented personal or institutional connection to Katori, Ye or the lattice-clock community. My field of electronic-structure theory and magnetism is close to B053 and B026, which I disclose as scientific proximity only, not a conflict. Since I now prefer B057, neither proximity affects my preferred configuration; I have no relationship to the Hall laboratory raised in Kroll's disclosure.
